paper.title: ICPL: Few-shot In-context Preference Learning via LLMs
paper.source_version: RLC/RLJ 2026 pre-proceedings Paper25.pdf retrieved 2026-08-30, SHA-256 58c7ec8c7412af61aa8de26b02416258e9ba9b74937db544484e3f4dcbcbdbc1; arXiv v3 revised 2025-04-03, PDF SHA-256 94c4347334940f8d53d7df32372e8eab5ad98bcb54044faa01d410f438dbd0d1; official code pinned to untagged public main HEAD a23c3bc0bbd29ad21ac33e29260f0ab8eb58c435 (2024-09-30), verified 2026-08-30.

decision_relevance.why_admitted: ICPL directly searches executable task-reward programs around repeated policy training and converts best/worst behavior preferences plus reward-component traces into the next reward proposal. It supplies a core outer-loop mechanism and exposes evaluation, reproducibility, and execution boundaries that matter when Sam keeps the trainer fixed.
not_evidence_for: Reference-dataset composition, motion selection, phase clocks, hybrid modes, guards, transitions, or recovery oracles
Natural-language steering, because paper participants select video identifiers and explanatory text feedback is future work
An untouched holdout evaluator, because the proxy sparse metric both selects candidates and reports performance
A single fixed trainer across baselines, because ICPL and PrefPPO use PPO while PEBBLE and SURF use SAC
Identical initialization, seeds, software versions, or compute for every candidate and baseline
Safe or sandboxed execution of generated reward code
Reward transfer across controllers, optimizers, simulators, observation contracts, or training budgets
Sim-to-real reward transfer or real-robot deployment
Broad human-preference generalization from seven training participants and one twenty-person final comparison

mechanisms.name: Reward design problem with preferences
mechanisms.description: The paper separates an MDP with preferences, reward-function space, learning algorithm A_M that maps a reward to a policy, and a preference set; the target is a reward whose trained policy best complies with those preferences.

mechanisms.name: Iterative executable reward-program search
mechanisms.description: A coding LLM receives task text and observation/action environment context, resamples until K reward functions execute, trains a separate PPO policy for each candidate, and repeats for N rounds without fitting a parametric reward model.

mechanisms.name: Good/bad reward context update
mechanisms.description: Humans rank candidate-policy videos; the code for the most and least preferred rewards is inserted as positive and negative context for the next reward generation round.

mechanisms.name: Component traces and historical-difference feedback
mechanisms.description: The next prompt includes component values for selected good and bad rewards, learning traces for prior good rewards, and another LLM's description of differences between consecutive good reward programs.

mechanisms.name: Index-only comparative human steering
mechanisms.description: A participant watches final-policy videos and selects best and worst identifiers. The signal steers the reward generator rather than directly commanding the low-level policy; explanatory language was not part of the reported study.

mechanisms.name: Sparse-metric proxy preference selector
mechanisms.description: In synthetic trials, an independent human-designed sparse task metric labels the highest-RTS reward as good and the lowest as bad; its values and functional form are not placed in the LLM prompt.

mechanisms.name: Per-candidate policy retraining
mechanisms.description: Within an IsaacGym task, candidate rewards reuse the reported task observation/action configuration and PPO training path, but each reward launches a new policy training run; the public sources do not prove a complete byte-identical trainer, seed, and budget manifest.

mechanisms.name: Generated-Python training loop
mechanisms.description: The pinned release extracts the first generated Python function, maps its arguments to environment attributes, appends it to a task module, launches IsaacGym training in a subprocess, retries failed candidates, parses traces and task scores, and evaluates selected code under five seeds.

failure_modes.name: Video-only preference ambiguity
failure_modes.description: Anymal was excluded from human trials because random-command following was difficult to judge from video. Direction, pose, and target-orientation visibility also caused documented ranking errors.

failure_modes.name: Minimal-metric leg-lift exploit
failure_modes.description: A one-leg jump satisfies a simple height criterion but fails the intended human-like style. Human preference rejected it, yet the study supplies no independent naturalness or physical-quality gate.

failure_modes.name: Initial reward diversity dependence
failure_modes.description: The authors report that qualitative task performance depends on diversity in the initial LLM reward batch; the method relies on the model to supply that diversity.

failure_modes.name: Limited human-study breadth
failure_modes.description: Seven people generated training preferences and twenty people judged one final HumanoidJump pair, limiting evidence for population-level preference robustness.

failure_modes.name: Nested policy-training latency
failure_modes.description: Every candidate requires a new RL run and each human-feedback round waits for training. The paper reports several-hour waits, 16.4 hours for the representative Humanoid ICPL run, and two-to-three-day human experiments.

failure_modes.name: Nested best-of-N reporting
failure_modes.description: FTS selects maxima over fixed-interval checkpoints, six candidates, five rounds, and five independent experiments. The publisher version explicitly says the metric reflects the strongest candidate rather than an average run.

failure_modes.name: Proxy metric reused for search and evaluation
failure_modes.description: The sparse task metric is separate from generated reward code and hidden from the LLM, but it selects good/bad examples and supplies RTS, TS, and FTS. The protocol has no untouched objective holdout against metric overfitting.

failure_modes.name: Mixed trainer and feedback contracts
failure_modes.description: ICPL and PrefPPO use PPO, while PEBBLE and SURF use SAC; ICPL proxy selection uses sparse task metrics while baselines receive dense trajectory preferences. Query-efficiency results are therefore not a fully fixed-trainer reward-only comparison.

failure_modes.name: High LLM and training variance
failure_modes.description: The paper reports substantial dispersion, uses five repeated experiments, and recommends repetition; feedback ablations do not dominate every task despite the aggregate top-two claim.

failure_modes.name: No explanatory text-feedback experiment
failure_modes.description: Participants provide best/worst identifiers, not natural-language rationales. The authors list explanatory text feedback as future work, and the pinned release defaults use_human_feedback to false.

failure_modes.name: Unsandboxed generated reward execution
failure_modes.description: The release parses only the first function signature, writes the generated body into an environment module, and runs it in a policy-training subprocess. It provides no import/AST allowlist, side-effect proof, resource boundary, or reward DSL.

failure_modes.name: Incomplete runtime identity
failure_modes.description: The Git commit is exact, but hosted model aliases and several Python dependencies are mutable; README and setup.py also disagree on the minimum Python version.

failure_modes.name: Hard-coded third-party LLM endpoint
failure_modes.description: The release constructs the OpenAI client with https://api.openai-proxy.com/v1 even though its README only instructs users to supply an OpenAI API key. Environment context and reward-history prompts therefore route through an endpoint outside the documented trust boundary.

failure_modes.name: Publisher/arXiv result drift
failure_modes.description: The active RLJ pre-proceedings and arXiv v3 are not byte- or value-identical. For example, PEBBLE-49 Quadcopter is -0.901 in RLJ Table 1 and -1.191 in arXiv v3 Table 1, so claims require an exact source version.

evaluation.name: Nine-task proxy-preference benchmark
evaluation.description: Five independent experiments compare ICPL, PrefPPO, PEBBLE, SURF, and a modified Eureka on nine IsaacGym tasks. ICPL uses sparse task metrics for proxy best/worst labels; PbRL baselines use dense preference labels.

evaluation.name: 49-query versus PbRL budget comparison
evaluation.description: ICPL's K=6, N=5 ranking protocol is counted as 49 pairwise queries and compared with PbRL budgets through 15,000; the paper reports at least a 30-fold reduction at equivalent or better scores.

evaluation.name: Trace, difference, bad-example, and OpenLoop ablations
evaluation.description: Ablations remove reward traces, then historical differences, then bad examples; OpenLoop samples K times N rewards without feedback. Full ICPL is reported top-two on eight of nine tasks, with high variance.

evaluation.name: Selected-task reward improvement over rounds
evaluation.description: Average RTS relative to round one is plotted for Ant and ShadowHand, the two tasks with the largest gaps over OpenLoop; the trend improves after multiple rounds but is not a nine-task monotonicity test.

evaluation.name: Real-human five-task IsaacGym trial
evaluation.description: Five video-rankable IsaacGym tasks use real best/worst selections. The paper reports an 18.4% average improvement over OpenLoop and says ICPL-real outperforms it on three of five tasks, with documented judgment errors.

evaluation.name: Subjective HumanoidJump preference comparison
evaluation.description: After five six-round, six-sample experiments, twenty additional volunteers compare randomized final videos; seventeen prefer ICPL and three prefer OpenLoop. The evidence is one simulated final pair without an independent naturalness metric.

evaluation.name: Paper and public-release audit
evaluation.description: The pinned untagged release matches the five-by-six search defaults but defaults to mutable GPT-4o, temperature 1.0, 3000 policy iterations, and five final evaluations; it directly executes generated Python and leaves key runtime dependencies unpinned.

evidence.claim: The current arXiv title and eight authors are recorded in v3; v1 was submitted 2024-10-22, v2 on 2025-01-31, and v3 on 2025-04-03.
The publisher lists the paper in Reinforcement Learning Journal volume 7 for RLC 2026 and states that the public file is pre-proceedings subject to minor changes.
The RDPP separates the MDP, reward space, learning algorithm, and preferences; ICPL generates executable rewards, trains agents, ranks behavior videos, and feeds selected rewards back to the LLM.
ICPL resamples to K executable reward functions, uses K=6 over N=5 PPO rounds, and feeds component evaluations, historical reward differences, and reward traces to the LLM.

The paper defines one query as a pairwise comparison, derives Q=49, lists larger budgets and nine tasks, defines the RTS/TS/FTS hierarchy over five experiments, and reports GPT-4-0613, GPT-4o, and one A100.

Sparse metrics select ICPL proxy good/bad examples, dense rewards label PbRL baselines, Table 1 reports exact task scores, the paper claims at least 30-fold query reduction, and modified Eureka uses six executable candidates.

evidence.locator: Section 5.5 and Tables 2 and 5, PDF pp. 7–11
evidence.claim: The paper ablates reward traces, differences, bad examples, and all feedback; acknowledges high variance and best-of-N selection; plots round improvement on selected Ant and ShadowHand tasks; and separately reports mean TS.

Seven volunteers produced human-loop preferences, twenty more evaluated methods, Anymal was excluded as hard to judge from video, and the paper reports five-task proxy and real-human results with 27.4% and 18.4% average improvements.

A leg-lift jump exploits a minimal height criterion; human feedback steers later two-leg behavior; five six-round, six-sample experiments precede a randomized comparison in which 17 of 20 voters prefer ICPL.
The authors list video-evaluation difficulty, absent explanatory text feedback, dependence on initial reward diversity, limited participants, and several-hour policy-retraining waits as limitations.

evidence.locator: Appendices A–B, full prompts and Algorithm 1
evidence.claim: The v3 supplement gives the total-plus-component code prompt, executable-resampling loop, selected good/bad code, reward traces, and LLM-generated differences between consecutive good rewards.
The supplement lists observation and action dimensions, task descriptions, and sparse task metrics for all nine IsaacGym tasks.

evidence.locator: Appendices E–F, training-time table and human setup
evidence.claim: The supplement reports 16.4 hours for ICPL on Humanoid, two-to-three-day human experiments, participant demographics, video-only task judgments, and an example of a mistaken Humanoid ranking.
The official project page summarizes the generate/train/rank/refine loop, query formula, fixed-interval checkpoint metric, human-study setup, and demonstrations.
The repository self-identifies as official; commit a23c3bc was the untagged public main HEAD verified on 2026-08-30, and the README names Python and IsaacGym requirements.
Release defaults are GPT-4o, temperature 1.0, simple-human preference, environment feedback on, text human feedback off, five rounds, six samples, 3000 policy iterations, and five final evaluations.
The prompt requests TorchScript-style Python returning total reward and a component dictionary and restricts declared reward inputs to exposed environment attributes.

The release extracts the first function, appends generated code to a task module, launches training in a subprocess, retries failed candidates, and performs no side-effect or import allowlist validation.
The release accepts best/worst identifiers, automatically selects proxy max/min task scores, assembles reward history, records selected code, and evaluates the best program in five seeded runs.
Package version 1.0 pins gym and caps torch but leaves OpenAI, NumPy, and several dependencies open; setup.py and README disagree on Python >=3.7 versus >=3.8.
The release constructs its OpenAI client with the hard-coded base URL https://api.openai-proxy.com/v1 rather than the default official API endpoint.
